Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

I have failed in my most important role in life
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'physical abuse by romantic partner', the appraisal 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' is clinically hard to reconcile because this trauma does not ordinarily involve other deaths or a mass-casualty context. The rest of the profile centers on partner violence, hypervigilance, and fragmented visual recall, so this item introduces a markedly different trauma scenario without support elsewhere in the selected items.

'Car sounds' is difficult to connect clinically to the rest of this profile for physical abuse by a romantic partner. The other trigger items and all threat, memory, and appraisal items center on interpersonal trauma, bodily alarm, betrayal, and fragmented terror-based recall. A car-sound trigger suggests a different trauma context unless there is supporting material elsewhere, so this item is the main coherence concern.

vignette:
Ravi had spent much of the first years of his marriage trying not to think in images. What he could not avoid were the moments that caught him unprepared: the stale, sweet smell of alcohol drifting out of a restaurant doorway, a burst of incomprehensible chatter in a crowded corridor, or the flat, sick feeling that came over him when he had a fever or an unsettled stomach. In each of those moments his body seemed to move before his mind could catch up. His chest tightened, his shoulders rose, and he found himself scanning for the nearest exit, already jumpy, already certain that something was wrong. As an architect, he worked in open-plan offices and spent time moving between noisy sites and meetings; when a subcontractor spoke over another in rapid, overlapping language, Ravi would go rigid and lose track of the conversation, then leave the room telling himself he needed air. He had come to believe that his own reactions were proof that he could not trust himself to do the right thing when it mattered, and that belief sat alongside a deeper shame: he had failed in his most important role in life by not keeping himself safe, and by failing to see what his partner was capable of until it was too late.

The trauma itself came back to him in fragments, each one sharp as a photograph. His former romantic partner had been drinking heavily that evening, and Ravi remembered the alcohol on his breath before he remembered the words. There had been a sudden barrage of angry speech, some of it blurred and impossible to follow, then the first blow and the sick, terror-filled awareness that he was trapped in a room with someone he had trusted. When he tried later to describe it, he could only manage a few moments at a time, each scene held in his mind as if he were looking at separate pictures: the raised hand, the overturned chair, the look on the other man's face. Remembering it brought back the same terror he had felt then, so vividly that his body would respond before he had fully formed the thought. A smell in a bar, a snatch of loud, indistinct conversation, or waking with a headache and fever would suddenly press the event back into the room with him. His pulse would race, his muscles would tense, and the memory would sharpen into those isolated still frames, making the abuse feel present rather than past. In those moments he became even more convinced that he had been naive, that he had betrayed his own judgment, and that his inability to see danger sooner meant he could not trust himself now.

Over time Ravi began to organise his days around staying ahead of that bodily alarm. He went to bed later and later because he needed to stay alert, listening for sounds in the house and checking the locks more than once, and lying awake only made him more jumpy the next day. When his body felt unwell-whether from a cold, a migraine, or simple exhaustion-he interpreted the sensation as the start of danger, and the unease spread quickly into the old terror. At work he avoided the lunch places where alcohol was served and declined client dinners whenever he could, quietly shrinking his social world. Even in his own office, a burst of incomprehensible chatter from the conference room could pull him back into the memory of being shouted at, and he would leave the door half-open, watch the hallway, and struggle to return to the plan on his screen. The more vigilant he became, the more readily his body reacted, and each reaction seemed to confirm that something terrible was near. That constant alertness made the memories more intrusive and more vivid; in turn, every flash of the event deepened his sense that he had failed and could not rely on his own judgment. He spoke of himself with a kind of grim certainty, saying that a man who had let betrayal happen once could not be counted on to protect his marriage or handle pressure at work.

By the time he came to therapy, Ravi was exhausted by the smallness of the life he had built around these alarms. His wife had noticed that he was withdrawn at home, hesitant to go out, and often preoccupied with scanning rooms and monitoring his own body. What brought him in was a recent episode after a flu-like illness, when feeling physically unwell triggered the old terror so strongly that he sat on the bathroom floor for nearly an hour, shaking and unable to settle. He said he was most afraid that this would never stop-that his body would keep warning him of danger before he could think, and that he would continue to live as though the betrayal were happening again. At the same time, he admitted a quieter hope: that if he could understand why alcohol smell, confused voices, and feeling ill were pulling him back into those stolen moments, he might begin to trust his own mind again and reclaim the parts of his marriage and work that fear had narrowed.
